newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's IMF package to end, no hurry on new pact.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's IMF package to end, no hurry on new pact.

text.p: Mexico is in no rush to seal a new deal to replace the contingency credit package from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) that was granted after the peso crashed in 1994, government officials said on Monday.
The $17.6 billion emergency loan package, originally approved by the IMF in February 1995, is set to expire this coming February 15.
The Mexican government is presently negotiating a medium-term Extended Fund Facility with the IMF, but officials said they were in no hurry to clinch the new deal.
"Clearly, there is no rush right now. This is mainly being done as a precautionary program for the medium-term," Finance Ministry spokesman Alejandro Valenzuela told Reuters.
Negotiations between Mexico and the IMF on an economic plan for the medium-term are on-going.
"What we are negotiating right now is to see what kind of numbers they need on our part," he said.

The earlier credit agreement, part of an overall multi-billion rescue package that helped bring Mexico back from the brink of financial collapse, had been extended for six months from last August on a request by the Mexican government.
Since receiving the IMF funds, Mexico has been paying them down, with the most recent payment coming in mid-January this year for $1.5 billion.

That left Mexico owing the IMF $11.61 billion, down from the $15.89 billion that the Mexican government owed at its peak on December 21 1995, Banco de Mexico said in statement released on January 15 this year.

Of the amount still owed only $827 million comes due in 1997, while $1.73 billion comes due in 1998, $5.9 billion in 1999, $3.09 billion in 2000 and smaller amounts after that, according to the Banco de Mexico, which is Mexico's central bank.
"The amount of money coming due from the IMF in 1999 and the year 2000 is quite large," Valenzuela said.
"What we want to do is have on a precautionary basis an amount that will put us in a comfortable position, particularly for the year 1999," he said.
Analysts said that the eventual signing of a new deal, expected to be three years long, could help boost Mexico's debt markets.

"When countries sign off on IMF agreements generically investors feel they have signed on for the program going forth for three years and that gives them a degree of comfort that there are some pre-set conditions and targets that have been agreed upon by the IMF," Merrill Lynch emerging market debt strategist Joyce Chang said.

"I don't think anyone actually feels that Mexico right now actually needs to use IMF financing at this particular point in time..., but I think that everybody appreciates that Mexico is thinking about their debt servicing going forward over the next couple of years," Chang told Reuters.

While government officials have declined to estimate what sort of numbers may be involved with the planned new IMF deal, Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz said last October that at that time they were talking about $6.0 billion.
He said this January that it was possible they would not have to use any precautionary IMF loan, particularly if the favorable conditions in capital markets continue as they have recently.
